_about: Explicit relationships between themes. 'why' explains the connection; 'tension' (optional) says where the two ideas pull in different directions or are easily confused. 'gurbani' lists line ids from gurbani.json that ground the link. All editorial; review status is tracked with the themes.

edges.why: Japji's second pauri joins them directly: whoever understands the Hukam no longer speaks from haumai. They are two ways of facing the same reality, from the narrow self or from the Order that holds everything.
Gurbani calls haumai an illness whose cure lies within it; the Salok goes on to name the cure as living by the Guru's Shabad, by grace. Naam is the daily form of that medicine.
Seva is one of the surest ways to loosen haumai, and one of the easiest places for it to hide.
edges.tension: Service done to be seen strengthens the ego it was meant to dissolve.

edges.why: Gurbani warns that reading and reflection can bind the seeker more tightly in self-conceit. Knowledge that does not humble is haumai in learned clothing.
The mind's desires (vasna) are haumai wanting things for itself. Turning the mind towards its source is how haumai is quietened.
Maya works through the mind: forgetting, attachment and the love of ‘the second’ are movements of a mind that has lost its source.
Gurbani speaks of Naam as revealed through the Guru's Shabad. Katha and sangat are where the Shabad is heard and Naam is kept.
Living in Naam and walking in the Hukam describe one alignment from two sides: remembrance from within, harmony with the Order from without.
In Gurmat, freedom comes through Naam and is completed by grace; the closing Salok of Japji speaks of those who meditated on Naam freeing many along with them.
Maya binds by making us forget; mukti is freedom from that forgetting while still living in the world.
edges.tension: Renunciation traditions treat leaving the world as the way out of Maya; Gurbani places freedom within household life.

edges.why: Babaji's katha moves between Vedanta texts and the language of devotion. Gurbani holds knowledge and love together.
edges.tension: In Advaita Vedanta, knowledge is the means of liberation and devotion is often preparatory; Gurbani keeps love and grace at the centre, even in the highest states.

edges.why: Love of the Divine shows itself in care for the Divine's creation; seva is devotion with hands.
In Gurmat, spiritual knowledge is the Guru's gift; it is received through the Shabad rather than achieved by learning alone.
Honest earning, sharing and service are rahini at its most concrete.
Gurbani holds both that we reap our own actions and that all happens within the Hukam. Responsibility and acceptance belong together.
edges.tension: Read carelessly, Hukam can sound like fatalism and karma like self-reliance; Gurmat accepts neither reading on its own.

edges.why: Gurbani's freedom is lived ‘while laughing, playing, dressing and eating’; conduct in ordinary life is where it is seen.
Babaji's Man Budh Atam series moves from the make-up of the mind to ‘what is the self’ and ‘what is knowledge’; one of its talks says outright that wanting obstructs knowledge.
